Reproducing Scherrer, Lynch et al. (2023) from dandiset 000691¶

Paper. Scherrer JR, Lynch GF, Zhang JJ, Fee MS (2023). An optical design enabling lightweight and large field-of-view head-mounted microscopes. Nature Methods 20, 546-549. doi:10.1038/s41592-023-01806-1. The version of record is not open access. This attempt used its abstract and the parts of its article page that are public: the figure titles, the Extended Data legends, and the data and code availability statements. The main text and the legends of Figures 1 and 2 were not available. The bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2021.09.03.458947, version 2) was read for its Methods only; no expected value comes from it.

Dandiset. DANDI:000691, version 0.260827.1358. The paper cites no DANDI version: its data statement points to an Academic Torrents deposit. This is the only published version. The draft holds the same two assets, with the same blobs and sizes (printed in the data check).

What the dandiset holds. One session of one mouse (4 mm cranial window, jGCaMP7f) imaged with the large-FOV microscope while it explores a looped corridor maze: the raw imaging video, 2948 EXTRACT footprints with traces and centroids, and a behaviour video (a second asset, an AVI). It holds no position of the mouse, no curation of the footprints, no pixel size, and none of the data of the other three mice, the three birds, or the optical tests.

Outside inputs. Two claims test the illumination profiles of Extended Data Fig. 2 on images the paper's code repository holds (GitHub FeeLab/Feescope-Paper-Code, commit d596646); they are data the dandiset does not hold. Every other result is computed from the dandiset alone. The parameters of the analysis come from the same code; see the helper module kiloscope.py.

Random numbers are drawn from a generator per claim section, each with its own fixed seed.

import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dandi.dandiapi import DandiAPIClient
from joblib import Parallel, delayed
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.decomposition import NMF

import kiloscope as ks

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 30)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

started = time.time()
urls = ks.asset_urls()
f = ks.open_nwb(urls)
S = ks.load_session(f)
print(f"NWB loaded in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
video_url = next(u for p, u in urls.items() if p.endswith(".avi"))
t0 = time.time()
# Frames kept for display: four in the opening part the code leaves out, four after it.
SAMPLE_FRAMES = (0, 640, 1280, 1900, 4000, 8000, 12000, 15000)
# Decoders are fit in parallel; their random numbers are drawn in order first, so results do not
# depend on the number of workers.
track = ks.track_mouse(video_url, keep_frames=SAMPLE_FRAMES)
B = ks.behaviour(S["t_img"], S["t_video"], track)
print(f"behaviour video decoded and tracked in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

The device description names the large-FOV microscope (Kiloscope) but gives the size and weight of the other one ("optimized for weight (1.0 mm FOV; 1.0 g)"), and the dandiset description also says the data come from "our microscope optimized for weight". The data are from the large-FOV microscope: a 4 mm window (the surgery field), thousands of footprints (below), and frames of 808 x 608 pixels, the size used for the Kiloscope in the paper's code (sf3/widefield/analysis.m, w = 808; h = 608). The imaging is stored as a TwoPhotonSeries and the dandiset lists "two-photon microscopy technique", but the microscope is a one-photon head-mounted epifluorescence microscope. The imaging plane gives the indicator and location as "unknown" and no excitation wavelength or pixel size, although general/virus says GCaMP7f. The plane segmentation has only image_mask and ROICentroids: there is no column that marks the footprints kept by the paper's curation. The segmentation parameters record cellfind_min_snr = 2, as the preprint's Methods state for the Kiloscope data.

def rate_summary(t):
    dt = np.diff(t)
    return {"n": len(t), "first_s": round(t[0], 3), "last_s": round(t[-1], 3),
            "median_dt_ms": round(1000 * np.median(dt), 2), "rate_hz": round(1 / np.median(dt), 2),
            "min_dt_ms": round(1000 * dt.min(), 2), "max_dt_ms": round(1000 * dt.max(), 2),
            "within_10pct": round(float(np.mean(np.abs(dt / np.median(dt) - 1) < 0.1)), 3)}

The imaging runs at a median 29.7 frames/s over 1234 s, as the series description says (about 30 frames/s), with irregular intervals (printed above). The behaviour video's timestamps run at a median of about 12.5 frames/s over the same 1234 s, while its description says about 30 frames/s and the AVI header says 30 frames/s. The AVI has as many frames as the NWB file has timestamps for it, so the timestamps are taken as the true frame times: at 30 frames/s the AVI would last only 517 s, less than half the imaging. The traces are stored as "df/F" with unit "n.a."; the EXTRACT parameters set trace_output_option to non-negative, which fits the three-quarters of values that are exactly zero. Their scale is not used below beyond moving maxima and normalized profiles.

# Which movie axis each centroid column indexes, and whether traces, masks and movie share a clock.
movie = f["acquisition/TwoPhotonSeries/data"]
masks = f["processing/ophys/ImageSegmentation/PlaneSegmentation/image_mask"]
rng_check = np.random.default_rng(691_00)
active = np.argsort(T[:2400].std(0))[::-1]
picked = active[:6]
controls = rng_check.choice(active[200:], size=6, replace=False)
n_check = 2400
lags = np.arange(-15, 16)

def hp(v):
    return v - pd.Series(v).rolling(301, center=True, min_periods=1).median().to_numpy()

def xcorr(a, b):
    out = []
    for L in lags:
        if L >= 0:
            out.append(np.corrcoef(a[L:], b[:len(b) - L])[0, 1])
        else:
            out.append(np.corrcoef(a[:L], b[-L:])[0, 1])
    return np.array(out)

rows = []
for i, j in zip(picked, controls):
    c0, c1 = S["centroids"][i]
    win = masks[i, max(c0 - 8, 0):c0 + 9, max(c1 - 8, 0):c1 + 9]
    peak = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(win), win.shape)
    patch = hp(movie[:n_check, c0 - 2:c0 + 3, c1 - 2:c1 + 3].astype(float).mean((1, 2)))
    own, other = hp(T[:n_check, i].astype(float)), hp(T[:n_check, j].astype(float))
    xo, xc = xcorr(patch, own), xcorr(patch, other)
    rows.append({"footprint": i, "mask_peak_offset": (peak[0] - min(c0, 8), peak[1] - min(c1, 8)),
                 "mask_max": round(float(win.max()), 3), "r_own_lag0": round(xo[15], 3),
                 "best_lag_frames": int(lags[np.nanargmax(xo)]), "r_own_best": round(np.nanmax(xo), 3),
                 "r_other_footprint_lag0": round(xc[15], 3)})
print("Movie pixels (5 x 5 at each centroid, first 2400 frames, slow drift removed) against traces:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

The centroids index the movie as (axis 1, axis 2) = (first column, second column): at each centroid the footprint's mask peaks at it or one pixel away (offsets printed above). The movie pixels at a footprint's centroid follow its own trace (r = 0.30 to 0.87 at lag 0, with the best lag within 2 frames for five of the six and 9 frames for one, where r rises only from 0.579 to 0.611), and do not follow the trace of another footprint (r = -0.15 to 0.07), so the traces come from this movie on its clock. These are the six footprints with the most variable traces; the check covers the first 2400 frames only (80 s), as the movie is chunked 1200 frames at a time.

The dandiset gives no position, so it is tracked here from the AVI with the code's colour rule. The mouse runs 48.5 loop lengths, in both directions, and visits all four arms (printed above). After frame 1920 every frame has a dark blob in the maze. Between consecutive video frames the blob moves 2.2 pixels at the median and 18.2 at the 99.9th percentile. Two steps exceed 40 pixels: a jump of 112 pixels at 1064.8 s and back in the next frame, with blobs of 8, 3 and 7 pixels. 55 frames have a blob under 50 pixels. Leaving those frames and both ends of the jump out changes the arm of 0.05% of the imaging frames, the octant of 0.06%, the running label of 1.07% and the direction of 0.18%. The largest step between imaging frames is 62 of 905 pixels. In the eight sample frames the tracked centroid lies on the mouse. The first 1920 frames (153 s on the timestamps) are left out, as in the code ("experimenter futzing"). Of the four sample frames from that part, the one at 102 s shows a gloved hand over the maze and a different camera view, and the one at 0 s shows the maze at another place in the frame; the other two look like the later frames.

Offsets of a second or two cannot be told apart by this check.

# Footprints deposited twice: pairs with near-identical traces and nearby centroids.
Z = (T - T.mean(0)) / T.std(0)
C = (Z.T @ Z) / len(Z)
np.fill_diagonal(C, 0)
iu = np.triu_indices_from(C, 1)
corr = C[iu]
dist = np.hypot(*(S["centroids"][iu[0]] - S["centroids"][iu[1]]).T)
for thr in [0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95]:
    k = corr > thr
    print(f"pairs with trace correlation > {thr}: {k.sum()}; of them within 10 px: {(k & (dist <= 10)).sum()}; "
          f"median centroid distance {np.median(dist[k]) if k.any() else float('nan'):.0f} px")
print("largest trace correlation between two footprints:", round(float(corr.max()), 3))
dup = (corr > 0.9) & (dist <= 10)
parent = np.arange(T.shape[1])
def find(a):
    while parent[a] != a:
        parent[a] = parent[parent[a]]
        a = parent[a]
    return a
for a, b in zip(iu[0][dup], iu[1][dup]):
    parent[find(a)] = find(b)
n_distinct = len({find(a) for a in range(T.shape[1])})
print("footprints after merging near-duplicates (r > 0.9, within 10 px):", n_distinct)
del Z, C

def decoding_report(real, null, names):
    per_real, per_null = np.nanmedian(real, 1), np.nanmedian(null, 1)
    print("classes absent from a test half (counted out of", real.size, "):", int(np.isnan(real).sum()))
    print(pd.DataFrame({"class": names, "mean_accuracy": np.nanmean(real, 0).round(3),
                        "null_mean": np.nanmean(null, 0).round(3),
                        "null_95th": np.nanpercentile(null, 95, axis=0).round(3)}).to_string(index=False))
    med, q95 = np.median(per_real), np.percentile(per_null, 95)
    print(f"median class accuracy per decoder: median {med:.3f} (range {per_real.min():.3f} to {per_real.max():.3f}); "
          f"null median {np.median(per_null):.3f}, 95th percentile {q95:.3f}; chance {1 / len(names):.3f}")
    print(f"ratio to chance {med * len(names):.2f}; real decoders above the null's 95th percentile: {(per_real > q95).sum()} of {len(per_real)}")
    print(f"code's summary (median of the averaged matrix's diagonal): {np.median(np.nanmean(real, 0)):.3f}")
    return med, q95

Result: reproduced. Over 50 decoders the median class accuracy for arm and direction is 0.415 (0.304 to 0.604), against chance at 0.125 and a 95th percentile of 0.145 for decoders with shifted labels; all 50 exceed it. This is 3.32 times chance. Two classes (arm 2 and arm 3 in the negative direction) reach only 0.239 and 0.236, the other six 0.443 to 0.594. With all frames in place of running frames the median is 0.348, against a null 95th percentile of 0.127. The SGD solver stops far from the optimum of its objective: on six splits it reaches objectives of 2.04 to 3.21, where an exact solver reaches 0.086 to 0.118 (at its limit of 10,000 iterations in all six). The exact solver gives lower accuracies for the three real decoders (0.262 to 0.318, against 0.443 to 0.535 with SGD) and 0.131 to 0.164 for the three with shifted labels, so with it too the real decoders are above chance and above every shifted one checked. The code fits these decoders with MATLAB's default for more than 100 predictors, 10 passes of dual SGD, which is also a truncated solver.

ed9c-local-decoding-map¶

Decoders that use the 32 footprints closest to a point, within 270 um, decode octant position significantly (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate 5%) in parts of the field of view, and accuracy differs across the field of view.

Criterion: grid every 30 pixels; points with at least 32 centroids within 45 pixels (270 um at 5.94 um per pixel); 10 decoders and 10 shifted-label decoders per point; one-sided z-test against the shifted decoders, Benjamini-Hochberg 5%; reproduced when at least one point is significant and the significant points' scores range over at least 0.05.

Decoders on 32 or 64 footprints are fit by an exact solver of the stated objective, as MATLAB does by default for 100 or fewer predictors (see the helper module). The first round of this attempt used 10 passes of SGD here; that solver is shown as a variant.

In [15]:
def local_map(n_near, radius_px, spacing, n_dec, seed, solver=None):
    """Grid points with at least n_near centroids within radius_px; at each, n_dec decoders and
    n_dec shifted-label decoders on its n_near nearest footprints, each point with its own
    generator spawned from the seed, run in parallel."""
    cen = S["centroids"].astype(float)
    points = []
    for a in np.arange(cen[:, 0].min(), cen[:, 0].max() + 1, spacing):
        for b in np.arange(cen[:, 1].min(), cen[:, 1].max() + 1, spacing):
            d = np.hypot(cen[:, 0] - a, cen[:, 1] - b)
            if (d <= radius_px).sum() >= n_near:
                points.append((a, b, int((d <= radius_px).sum()), np.argsort(d)[:n_near]))
    seeds = np.random.SeedSequence(seed).spawn(len(points))
    fits = Parallel(n_jobs=-1)(delayed(ks.local_decoders)(X_run[:, idx], labels_oct, ks.LAMBDA_OCTANT, n_dec, s, solver)
                               for (_, _, _, idx), s in zip(points, seeds))
    rows = []
    for (a, b, n_within, _), fit in zip(points, fits):
        real, null = fit["real"], fit["null"]
        z = (real.mean() - null.mean()) / null.std(ddof=1)
        rows.append({"c0": a, "c1": b, "score": real.mean(), "null_mean": null.mean(), "null_sd": null.std(ddof=1),
                     "z": z, "p": stats.norm.sf(z), "n_within": n_within, "at_iteration_limit": fit["at_iteration_limit"],
                     # Variant test: Welch's t-test of the 10 real against the 10 shifted decoders, one-sided.
                     "p_t": stats.ttest_ind(real, null, equal_var=False, alternative="greater").pvalue})
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    out["q_bh"] = stats.false_discovery_control(out.p.to_numpy())
    out["significant"] = out.q_bh < 0.05
    out["significant_t"] = stats.false_discovery_control(out.p_t.to_numpy()) < 0.05
    return out

def map_report(m, label):
    sig = m[m.significant]
    print(f"{label}: {len(m)} grid points used; significant at BH 5%: {len(sig)} ({len(sig) / len(m):.0%})")
    print(f"  score over all points {m.score.min():.3f} to {m.score.max():.3f} (median {m.score.median():.3f}); "
          f"null means {m.null_mean.min():.3f} to {m.null_mean.max():.3f}")
    print(f"  null standard deviation per point, percentiles 5/50/95: {np.round(np.percentile(m.null_sd, [5, 50, 95]), 4)}; "
          f"z percentiles 5/50/95: {np.round(np.percentile(m.z, [5, 50, 95]), 2)}; largest z {m.z.max():.2f}, smallest q {m.q_bh.min():.3f}")
    print(f"  z the best point needs to pass alone (p < 0.05 / {len(m)}): {stats.norm.isf(0.05 / len(m)):.2f}")
    print(f"  exact fits that reached the iteration limit: {m.at_iteration_limit.sum()} of {20 * len(m)}")
    if len(sig):
        print(f"  significant points' scores {sig.score.min():.3f} to {sig.score.max():.3f} (range {sig.score.max() - sig.score.min():.3f}); "
              f"smallest z among them {sig.z.min():.2f}")
    sig_t = m[m.significant_t]
    print(f"  variant, Welch t-test in place of the z-test: significant at BH 5%: {len(sig_t)}"
          + (f"; scores {sig_t.score.min():.3f} to {sig_t.score.max():.3f} (range {sig_t.score.max() - sig_t.score.min():.3f})" if len(sig_t) else ""))

t0 = time.time()
radius = 45       # 270 um at 5.94 um per pixel, rounded to 45 pixels as in the criterion

print(f"computed in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; radius {radius} px; exact solver (32 predictors)")
map_report(amap, "32 footprints within 270 um")

cen = S["centroids"].astype(float)
picked_points = amap.iloc[np.linspace(0, len(amap) - 1, 4).astype(int)]
seeds = np.random.SeedSequence(691_11).spawn(4)
rows = []
for (_, pt), s in zip(picked_points.iterrows(), seeds):
    idx = np.argsort(np.hypot(cen[:, 0] - pt.c0, cen[:, 1] - pt.c1))[:32]
    rows.append({"c0": pt.c0, "c1": pt.c1, **ks.solver_check(X_run[:, idx], labels_oct, 8, ks.LAMBDA_OCTANT, np.random.default_rng(s), max_iter=100000)})
print("SGD and exact solver on the same split (exact up to 100,000 iterations); objective = summed mean hinge + penalty:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("For reference, predicting every class as absent (w = 0, b = -1) gives an objective of 2 * (sum of class fractions) = 2.0")

Result: reproduced. With the 32 footprints closest to a point within 270 um (45 pixels), 150 grid points qualify and 18 of them (12%) are significant at Benjamini-Hochberg 5%, with scores of 0.112 to 0.187, a range of 0.075 where the criterion asks for 0.05. Over all points the scores run from 0.068 to 0.187 (median 0.125), against null means of 0.065 to 0.123. The result depends on the solver. With 10 passes of SGD, as in the first round of this attempt, on the same points and seeds, 1 point is significant and the criterion is not met; at four points checked, SGD stops at objectives of 19.8 to 68.9, where the exact solver reaches 1.976 to 2.000. That optimum is close to the objective of predicting every class absent (2.0), so the scores rest on weak classifiers. liblinear reached its limit of 10,000 iterations in 2268 of the 3000 fits. Each point's null standard deviation comes from 10 shifted decoders (0.018 to 0.046, 5th to 95th percentile); a point alone needs z above 3.40, and the smallest z among the significant points is 2.53. A Welch t-test of the 10 real against the 10 shifted decoders, in place of the z-test, marks 80 points significant (scores 0.108 to 0.187, range 0.079); with SGD it marks 5 (range 0.052). With the code's choice, 64 footprints within 50 pixels on a 60 pixel grid (the criterion's 40 pixel grid was not run, to keep within the time limit), 22 of 34 points are significant, with scores of 0.141 to 0.211 (range 0.070), and 32 with the t-test. The map was not rerun with more decoders per point: it takes about 640 s with 10. As the exact fits stop at an iteration limit, the counts can differ slightly between machines.

ed10-localized-activity¶

Some footprints have activity localized to subregions of the maze.

Criterion: entropy of each footprint's mean activity over 100 bins of linear position, in frames above the 80th percentile of speed; localized when below all of 100 values with position shifted against activity; reproduced when the number localized exceeds the count expected at 1/101 with binomial p < 0.001.

In [17]:
rng_pf = np.random.default_rng(691_07)
fast = B["speed"] > np.percentile(B["speed"], 80)
s_run = B["s"][fast]
lo, hi = np.percentile(s_run, [1, 99])
bins = np.clip(np.floor(np.clip((s_run - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 0.999) * 100), 0, 99).astype(int)
A = T[B["sel"]][fast].astype(np.float64)
n = len(bins)

def entropies(bin_labels):
    onehot = np.zeros((100, n)); onehot[bin_labels, np.arange(n)] = 1
    occ = onehot.sum(1)
    mean_act = (onehot @ A) / np.maximum(occ, 1)[:, None]
    p = mean_act / mean_act.sum(0)
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        return -np.nansum(np.where(p > 0, p * np.log2(p), 0), axis=0), occ

obs, occ = entropies(bins)
print(f"frames above the 80th percentile of speed: {n}; frames per bin {occ.min():.0f} to {occ.max():.0f}")
nulls = np.array([entropies(np.roll(bins, int(rng_pf.integers(n // 10, n - n // 10))))[0] for _ in range(100)])
below = (nulls <= obs).sum(0)
n_fp = A.shape[1]
expected = n_fp / 101
for k, label in [(0, "below all 100 (criterion)"), (5, "at most 5 null values below (p <= 0.06)")]:
    count = int((below <= k).sum())
    fp_rate = (k + 1) / 101
    p_binom = stats.binomtest(count, n_fp, fp_rate, alternative="greater").pvalue
    print(f"{label}: {count} of {n_fp} footprints ({count / n_fp:.1%}); expected by chance {n_fp * fp_rate:.0f}; binomial p = {p_binom:.2g}")
print(f"entropy, bits (maximum log2(100) = {np.log2(100):.2f}): observed median {np.median(obs):.3f}, "
      f"range {obs.min():.3f} to {obs.max():.3f}; null median {np.median(nulls):.3f}")
# Empirical false-positive count: each shifted copy in turn treated as the observed data and
# compared with the other 99 (the same shifts serve every footprint, so counts are correlated).
loo = np.array([int((np.delete(nulls, j, 0) > nulls[j]).all(0).sum()) for j in range(100)])
print(f"shifted copy as observed, below all 99 others: count per copy median {np.median(loo):.0f}, 95th percentile "
      f"{np.percentile(loo, 95):.0f}, maximum {loo.max()} (expected {n_fp / 100:.0f}); copies with a count of at least "
      f"{int((below == 0).sum())}: {(loo >= (below == 0).sum()).sum()} of 100")
gain = (nulls.mean(0) - obs)
print("entropy below the null mean, localized footprints, percentiles 5/50/95 (bits):",
      np.round(np.percentile(gain[below == 0], [5, 50, 95]), 3))
top = np.argsort(gain)[::-1][:6]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(14, 2), sharey=True)
for a_, i in zip(ax, top):
    prof = np.bincount(bins, weights=A[:, i], minlength=100) / np.maximum(occ, 1)
    a_.plot(prof / prof.max()); a_.set_title(f"footprint {i}", fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_ylabel("activity / max"); fig.supxlabel("linear position bin", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
print("Profiles are each scaled to their maximum (0 to 1).")

frames above the 80th percentile of speed: 6411; frames per bin 0 to 224

below all 100 (criterion): 100 of 2948 footprints (3.4%); expected by chance 29; binomial p = 4.5e-25
at most 5 null values below (p <= 0.06): 448 of 2948 footprints (15.2%); expected by chance 175; binomial p = 1.7e-72
entropy, bits (maximum log2(100) = 6.64): observed median 6.128, range 3.642 to 6.513; null median 6.183
shifted copy as observed, below all 99 others: count per copy median 28, 95th percentile 54, maximum 62 (expected 29); copies with a count of at least 100: 0 of 100
entropy below the null mean, localized footprints, percentiles 5/50/95 (bits): [0.201 0.448 0.899]

Profiles are each scaled to their maximum (0 to 1).

Result: reproduced. 100 of 2948 footprints (3.4%) have an entropy over linear position below all 100 values with position shifted, where 29 are expected by chance (binomial p = 4.5e-25); at a looser threshold, 448 against 175. The binomial p-value treats footprints as independent, but the same shifts serve every footprint. Treating each shifted copy in turn as the observed data gives counts with a median of 28, a 95th percentile of 54 and a maximum of 62; none of the 100 copies reaches the observed 100. The effect per footprint is small: for the 100, the entropy is 0.20 to 0.90 bits (5th to 95th percentile) below the mean of the shifted values, out of a maximum of 6.64 bits. The paper's examples were chosen by eye; they are not identified here.

ed8-coactive-distributed¶

The footprints that take part in a large correlated event of each NMF component are spread across the field of view.

Criterion: NMF with 8 components (4 replicates); each footprint to the component where its weight ranks highest; the event at the component's largest temporal weight; footprints active when their maximum within 25 s exceeds half their overall maximum; reproduced when at least 6 of 8 events have at least 10 active footprints with a spread at least half that of all footprints.

In [18]:
rng_nmf = np.random.default_rng(691_08)
t0 = time.time()
fits = []
for rep in range(4):
    model = NMF(8, solver="mu", init="random", max_iter=200, random_state=int(rng_nmf.integers(2**31)))
    W = model.fit_transform(T)
    fits.append((model.reconstruction_err_, W, model.components_))
err, W, H = min(fits, key=lambda z: z[0])
print(f"NMF in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; reconstruction errors {[round(z[0], 2) for z in fits]}")
rank = np.argsort(np.argsort(H, axis=1), axis=1)       # rank of each footprint within each component
group = rank.argmax(0)
cen_um = S["centroids"] * ks.UM_PER_PIXEL
def spread(p):
    return np.sqrt(((p - p.mean(0)) ** 2).sum(1).mean())
all_spread = spread(cen_um)
peak_all = T.max(0)
def events_table(threshold, t_from=0.0):
    rows = []
    for c in range(8):
        members = np.flatnonzero(group == c)
        later = S["t_trace"] >= t_from
        tpk = S["t_trace"][later][np.argmax(W[later, c])]
        win = np.abs(S["t_trace"] - tpk) <= 25
        act_ = members[T[win][:, members].max(0) > threshold * peak_all[members]]
        d = np.hypot(*(cen_um[act_][:, None, :] - cen_um[act_][None, :, :]).transpose(2, 0, 1)) if len(act_) > 1 else np.zeros((1, 1))
        rows.append({"component": c, "members": len(members), "event_t_s": round(tpk, 1), "active": len(act_),
                     "spread_ratio": round(spread(cen_um[act_]) / all_spread, 3) if len(act_) > 1 else np.nan,
                     "pairwise_90th_mm": round(np.percentile(d[np.triu_indices_from(d, 1)], 90) / 1000, 2) if len(act_) > 1 else np.nan})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
ev = events_table(0.5)
print(f"spread of all footprints: {all_spread / 1000:.2f} mm (RMS distance from their mean, at {ks.UM_PER_PIXEL} um/px)")
print(ev.to_string(index=False))
passing = int(((ev.active >= 10) & (ev.spread_ratio >= 0.5)).sum())
print(f"events with at least 10 active footprints and spread ratio >= 0.5: {passing} of 8")
for thr in (0.3, 0.7):
    e2 = events_table(thr)
    print(f"variant, active above {thr} of maximum: {int(((e2.active >= 10) & (e2.spread_ratio >= 0.5)).sum())} of 8; "
          f"spread ratios {e2.spread_ratio.min():.2f} to {e2.spread_ratio.max():.2f}")
ev_late = events_table(0.5, t_from=B["t"][0])
print(f"variant, event times from t = {B['t'][0]:.0f} s on (after the opening part the behaviour analysis leaves out): "
      f"{int(((ev_late.active >= 10) & (ev_late.spread_ratio >= 0.5)).sum())} of 8; event times {ev_late.event_t_s.tolist()}; "
      f"spread ratios {ev_late.spread_ratio.min():.2f} to {ev_late.spread_ratio.max():.2f}")

# Baselines: members active in randomly placed 50 s windows, and the spread of random sets of footprints.
rng_ed8 = np.random.default_rng(691_10)
t_tr = S["t_trace"]
rows = []
for c in range(8):
    members = np.flatnonzero(group == c)
    fracs = []
    for tc in rng_ed8.uniform(t_tr[0] + 25, t_tr[-1] - 25, 100):
        win = np.abs(t_tr - tc) <= 25
        fracs.append(np.mean(T[win][:, members].max(0) > 0.5 * peak_all[members]))
    n_act = int(ev.active[c])
    rand_spread = [spread(cen_um[rng_ed8.choice(len(cen_um), n_act, replace=False)]) / all_spread for _ in range(200)]
    rows.append({"component": c, "event_fraction_active": round(n_act / ev.members[c], 3),
                 "random_windows_median": round(float(np.median(fracs)), 3), "random_windows_95th": round(float(np.percentile(fracs, 95)), 3),
                 "event_spread_ratio": ev.spread_ratio[c], "random_set_spread_5th": round(float(np.percentile(rand_spread, 5)), 3),
                 "random_set_spread_95th": round(float(np.percentile(rand_spread, 95)), 3)})
print("\nBaselines (100 random 50 s windows per component; 200 random sets of footprints of the event's size):")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(12, 5))
for c, a_ in enumerate(ax.ravel()):
    members = np.flatnonzero(group == c)
    tpk = S["t_trace"][np.argmax(W[:, c])]
    win = np.abs(S["t_trace"] - tpk) <= 25
    act_ = members[T[win][:, members].max(0) > 0.5 * peak_all[members]]
    a_.scatter(S["centroids"][:, 1], S["centroids"][:, 0], s=1, color="0.8")
    a_.scatter(S["centroids"][act_, 1], S["centroids"][act_, 0], s=3, color="r")
    a_.set_title(f"component {c}: {len(act_)} active", fontsize=8); a_.invert_yaxis(); a_.set_aspect("equal"); a_.axis("off")
plt.show()

Result: reproduced. For all 8 NMF components the event has 196 to 320 active footprints, and their spread is 0.945 to 1.055 times that of all footprints, with a 90th percentile of pairwise distance of 2.05 to 2.29 mm at 5.94 um per pixel. Thresholds of 0.3 and 0.7 give 8 of 8 as well. Two events (80.4 and 122.9 s) fall in the opening 153 s that the behaviour analysis leaves out; with event times from 153 s on, 8 of 8 pass, with spread ratios of 0.94 to 1.05. The test separates these events from other times only in part. In 100 random 50 s windows the median fraction of a component's members that is active is 0.399 to 0.519, and the event's fraction (0.568 to 0.851) is above the 95th percentile of the random windows for 6 of the 8 components. Random sets of footprints of the event's size have spread ratios of 0.951 to 1.042 (5th to 95th percentiles, over components). The event's spread ratio lies within its own component's random range for 3 of the 8 components, below it for 2 (0.945 and 0.956, against 5th percentiles of 0.962) and above it for 3 (1.042, 1.055 and 1.050, against 95th percentiles of 1.037, 1.042 and 1.036). The active footprints are spread across the field of view, which is what the claim states; the criterion's threshold of half the overall spread is far below what any set of this size reaches.

ed2b-featherscope-flat-illumination and ed2c-kiloscope-flat-illumination¶

With the axicon correction optics the signal intensity profile is flat across the field of view, where total vignetting makes the signal fall toward the edges (Extended Data Fig. 2b for the Featherscope, 2c for the Kiloscope).

The images are measurements of a thin layer of fluorescent dye kept in the paper's code repository (they are data, not figures), read at commit d596646 as sf3/*/analysis.m reads them: corrected (axicons), optical vignetting (led), and total vignetting (reference). Criterion: the corrected profile at or above 0.8 out to 0.4 mm (Featherscope) or 1.5 mm (Kiloscope), and above the total-vignetting profile there.

In [19]:
setups = {
    "ed2b-featherscope": dict(folder="sf3/feather", um=1.68, max_um=500, med=3, R=400,
                              files={"corrected": "axicons/rgb2021-01-29T16_31_30.png", "optical vignetting": "led/feather.png",
                                     "total vignetting": "reference/rgb2021-01-29T16_54_50.png"}),
    "ed2c-kiloscope": dict(folder="sf3/widefield", um=5.94, max_um=2000, med=10, R=1500,
                           files={"corrected": "axicons/rgb2021-01-08T14_40_22.png", "optical vignetting": "led/rgb2021-01-29T15_25_25.png",
                                  "total vignetting": "reference/rgb2021-01-08T15_23_50.png"}),
}
profiles = {}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5))
for a_, (name, s) in zip(ax, setups.items()):
    profiles[name] = {}
    for label, fn in s["files"].items():
        img = ks.read_png(ks.code_file_url(f"{s['folder']}/{fn}"))
        img = ks.unpack_rgb565(img) if img.ndim == 3 else img.astype(float)
        prof = ks.radial_profile(img, s["um"], s["max_um"], s["med"])
        profiles[name][label] = prof
        a_.plot(prof, label=label)
        print(f"{name} {label}: image {img.shape}, values {img.min():.0f} to {img.max():.0f}")
    a_.set_xlim(0, s["max_um"]); a_.set_ylim(0, 1.1); a_.axvline(s["R"], color="k", ls=":")
    a_.set_xlabel("radius (um)"); a_.set_title(name); a_.legend(fontsize=7)
plt.show()
for name, s in setups.items():
    p = profiles[name]
    R = s["R"]
    rows = []
    for label, prof in p.items():
        rows.append({"profile": label, "min_0_to_R": round(np.nanmin(prof[:R + 1]), 3),
                     **{f"at_{r}um": round(prof[r], 3) for r in (R // 4, R // 2, 3 * R // 4, R)}})
    print(f"\n{name} (R = {R} um):")
    print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
    n_out = {label: int(np.sum(prof[:s['max_um']] > 1.1)) for label, prof in p.items()}
    print("radii with values above the plotted 1.1:", n_out)

# Sensitivity of the corrected profiles to the radius and the centre.
for name, s in setups.items():
    img = ks.read_png(ks.code_file_url(f"{s['folder']}/{s['files']['corrected']}"))
    img = ks.unpack_rgb565(img) if img.ndim == 3 else img.astype(float)
    xc, yc = ks.weighted_centre(img)
    h, w = img.shape
    step = round(100 / s["um"])       # 100 um in pixels
    centres = {"intensity-weighted (main)": (xc, yc), "image centre": ((w + 1) / 2, (h + 1) / 2),
               "weighted + 100 um in x": (xc + step, yc), "weighted - 100 um in x": (xc - step, yc),
               "weighted + 100 um in y": (xc, yc + step), "weighted - 100 um in y": (xc, yc - step)}
    rows = []
    for label, centre in centres.items():
        prof = ks.radial_profile(img, s["um"], s["max_um"], s["med"], centre=centre)
        row = {"centre": label, "x_px": round(centre[0], 1), "y_px": round(centre[1], 1)}
        for f_ in (0.95, 1.0, 1.05):
            r = round(f_ * s["R"])
            row[f"min_0_to_{r}um"] = round(np.nanmin(prof[:r + 1]), 3)
        rows.append(row)
    print(f"\n{name}, corrected profile, minimum out to R - 5%, R, R + 5%:")
    print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Result: partially reproduced, for both. With the correction optics the profile falls less toward the edge than with total vignetting: at 0.4 mm, 0.742 against 0.342 for the Featherscope; at 1.5 mm, 0.797 against 0.253 for the Kiloscope. Neither corrected profile stays at or above 0.8 out to that radius (minima 0.742 and 0.797, the Kiloscope's 0.003 short), so the "flat" part of the criterion is not met. Optical vignetting alone falls to 0.628 and 0.389 at the same radii. The minima depend on the radius and the centre. For the Featherscope the minimum is 0.785 out to 0.38 mm and 0.698 out to 0.42 mm; with the centre moved by 100 um it is 0.626 to 0.867, and 0.766 about the image centre. For the Kiloscope it is 0.846 out to 1.425 mm and 0.742 out to 1.575 mm; with the centre moved by 100 um it is 0.765 to 0.831 (above 0.8 for one of the four moves), and 0.695 about the image centre. The outcome uses the code's centre and the criterion's radius.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's.

  • The claims come from the abstract and the public Extended Data legends; the main text was not available.
  • All 2948 footprints are used, where the paper used the 2382 it kept after curation; the dandiset does not mark them.
  • The mouse's position is tracked here from the behaviour video with the code's colour rule, in the unrotated frame, with the loop's sides taken from the positions; the paper used its own tracking, which is not in the dandiset.
  • MATLAB's linear SVM is replaced by scikit-learn solvers of the same objective, chosen by MATLAB's default rule: SGD with 10 passes for the decoders on all footprints, an exact solver (liblinear) for the local decoders on 32 or 64 footprints. On six splits each for the quadrant and direction and the octant decoders, the exact solver gives lower accuracies, still above every shifted decoder checked. 50 decoders per analysis where the code ran 200.
  • The local map follows the legend (32 footprints within 270 um) on a 30 pixel grid with a z-test against 10 shifted decoders per point; the code's 64 footprints within 50 pixels is a variant, on a 60 pixel grid where the criterion says 40, to keep within the time limit. The paper's significance test is not described. The local map's outcome depends on the solver: with SGD, as in the first round of this attempt, it fails.
  • Event times for Extended Data Fig. 8 are each component's largest weight, where the code sets them by hand.

What was found about the dandiset.

  • It holds one of the paper's four mice and none of its bird or optical data. The Academic Torrents deposit the paper names holds the same mouse only.
  • The device description gives the weight-optimized microscope's size and weight (1.0 mm, 1.0 g) for the large-FOV one, and the dandiset description says the data come from the microscope optimized for weight; the data are from the large-FOV microscope.
  • The imaging is stored as a TwoPhotonSeries and listed as two-photon microscopy; the microscope is a one-photon head-mounted microscope.
  • The behaviour video is described as about 30 frames/s, and its AVI header says 30; its timestamps run at 12.5 frames/s, and only at that rate does it cover the imaging.
  • No pixel size, indicator, location or excitation wavelength; no curation of the footprints; no position of the mouse.
  • The traces, the raw movie and the behaviour timestamps are consistent with one another: the movie pixels at six footprints follow their traces (r = 0.30 to 0.87 at lag 0), and position decoding falls to chance when the labels are shifted by 20 s.
